content.text:
The question is about what your "one library" decision actually decided.

**What the two libraries are.** The interpreter has the full standard library, 4.5K lines, the one every microGPT program runs on. The compiler has its own small prelude, written 2008 as a "stripped-down minimalist library for first crack at compilation", a "hopefully temporary hack" in the team's words. On 2026-09-20 you decided the prelude is a bootstrap to get rid of: the interpreter's library becomes the one library the compiler checks, and the prelude's three files are deleted at the switch-over.

**Where the two differ on numbers.** In the interpreter's library the numbers nest: a `ZZ32` is a `ZZ64`, which is a `ZZ` (unbounded integer), which is a `QQ` (rational), which is an `RR64` (double), which is a `Number`. That is the mathematical picture, ℤ inside ℚ inside ℝ, and it is why `Number`'s catch-all operations serve every level and microGPT can mix integers and floats freely. In the compiler's prelude Steele flattened this in July 2011: `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and the rest sit side by side under `Number`, none a subtype of another, and a narrower value is widened by a declared `coerce` that the compiler inserts where needed. Every language you named as a peer (Java, Swift, Rust, Julia, X10) has the flat shape.

**Why it matters for the checker.** Each level of the nested tower declares "I am `Equality` at my own type", so one `ZZ32` is `Equality` at five different instantiations at once. The exclusion rule forbids exactly that, and it is 61 of the checker's 103 errors on the library. In the flat shape every type is `Equality` at one instantiation, the errors vanish, and the checker is not touched. That is route A: keep the rule, give the one library's tower the prelude's shape. The other two routes keep the nesting and change the checker instead.

**The reading that would rule A out.** The judge who examined rung P's finding struck A on this ground: you chose the interpreter's library, and A would reshape its tower into the prelude's, which he read as re-importing the prelude's design after deleting its files. Two of your own statements lean that way: "the library's own practice is the standard" (09-19), and your row 330 reasoning "ℤ sits under ℚ under ℝ64 in the tower". The brief's counter-reading: the decision as recorded settled which files survive, not that every design choice inside them is frozen.

**So the question is:** when you said "one library, the interpreter's", did you mean only the files, or also its nested numeric tower? If the tower is part of what you chose, A is out. Then B drops the specialisation shortcut, which you called a must, so C is what remains: the patents' forest rule, where the soundness rule is ours to derive, 40 to 70 lines with no source. In practice the question is "flatten the numbers, as the team did for the compiled world" against "build the type theory they sketched and never built".

- **POPL 2019 kept the rule for invariant traits and moved the return-type check to run time.** Park, Hong, Steele, Ryu, *Polymorphic symmetric multiple dispatch with variance*, PACMPL 3 (POPL), art. 11, doi:10.1145/3290324 (text from the Wayback copy of the ACM PDF). The core calculus FGFV has multiple inheritance, variance and reified dispatch. Its [Anc-Same-Trait] rule: "if a class C extends two instances of a trait T, T⟦α⟧ and T⟦ρ⟧, then C also extends some T⟦γ⟧ … that extends both … because the rules guarantee that there always exists a single minimal ancestor when a class extends multiple instances of a trait, no ambiguous method calls are possible due to multiple instances of a trait" (p. 11:11). For an invariant T only γ = α = ρ satisfies this (derived here, not stated there), so the invariant case of the exclusion stands, and the covariant case is Naden's "minimal instantiation" refinement.
---
- Typed Racket nests the tower statically ("Integer is a subtype of Rational, which is a subtype of Real") with union types and "overloading with intersection types". It names the tower as the hard case for typed languages: "No existing typed language provides as rich a numeric hierarchy nor as many generic operations as those found in Smalltalk, Scheme, or Racket" (St-Amour et al., *Typing the Numeric Tower*, PADL 2012, pp. 1-2, 5, https://www2.ccs.neu.edu/racket/pubs/padl12-stff.pdf). It has no self-typed traits and no run-time dispatch on type arguments.
- Apart from Naden's write-up and the 2012 patents, no source was found that treats a nested tower carrying self-typed traits at each level together with run-time dispatch over reified generics.

## What the field settled and what it did not

- **Keep the rule and flatten the tower.**
  - Java, Kotlin, Scala and X10 keep the rule, with flat numeric types and widening. Java's stated reason is erasure.
  - The Fortress group kept the rule after 2012 (Welterweight 2012, POPL 2019), for "unique minimal instance" dispatch.
  - Cecil's root-only `ordered[num]` and C#'s `INumber<TSelf>` on sibling structs are two flat shapes in use.
- **Drop the rule and instantiate at the call site with no specialised overloads.**
  - C#, F#, Rust and Haskell allow multiple instantiation, and every one chooses instances and overloads statically. None has run-time dispatch over generic overloads, the one place Naden's hole opens.
  - Ceylon allows variant multiple instantiation and has no overloading.
- **Neither route.**
  - Julia avoids the trade by single inheritance and gives up static soundness ("no notion of soundness"). It keeps specialised methods and moves ambiguity to a run-time error.
  - POPL 2019 keeps both the rule and specialisation by checking the static return type at run time, the option Naden rejected.
  - The 2012 patents' "Self-types meet … must form a forest" admits the tower's chain of self-typed instantiations inside the rule, close to the review's route C. It was never published, and its test (`comprises T`) is absent from the library's `Equality`.
- **Not settled.** Nobody published a resolution of the tower conflict under run-time dispatch, or a proof that the rule is necessary; the published proofs show only that it suffices.

Recorded in POSITIONS as reactions, not decisions (`b49f6a4ef`). Answers per question:

**1, coercion.** Today a `ZZ32` value *is* an `RR64`, so `Number`'s catch-all `+` takes both. Under coercion they are separate types, and the library declares a conversion, `RR64 coerce(z: ZZ32)`, which the compiler inserts wherever an `RR64` is expected and no declaration applies without it. That is the spec's own mechanism between `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, and the compiler prelude already runs on 15 such lines. What you keep: `x: RR64 = someInteger` works, mixed arithmetic works, row 330's decision stands with "promotion" restated as "coercion". What you give up: ℤ as a subtype of ℚ in the type relation itself, and `Empty extends List[\T\]`. The one known open item: generic code over mixed widths, where the join of a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` becomes a trait without arithmetic; the brief lists it as unsettled.

**2, the forest rule and POPL 2019.** A correction: the published path did not continue the forest route. POPL 2019 keeps the rule for invariant traits, allows two instantiations only when a single minimal ancestor exists (a cousin of the forest rule, for covariant traits), keeps specialisation by checking the return type at run time (the option Naden rejected), and has no self types and no numeric tower. So on the tower, the group's last published word is "rule kept, no nesting", which is A's shape. The forest rule survives only in the patents, filed on the last day and never built. Your "yes" stands as your weighting; the fact underneath it is narrower than you read it.

**3, which files survive.** Recorded. Route A stays on the table.

**4, the specialisation shortcut.** Two things get called specialisation. One: the class loader stamps out a class per type argument, like C++ templates. Every route keeps that, and unboxing will build on it. Two: a hand-written special version of a generic function for one instantiation under the same name, `dot(v: Vector[\RR64\])` beside `dot[\T\](v: Vector[\T\])`, picked at run time by the value's type. That is the shortcut; the exclusion rule exists to make it sound; B forbids it. Your "as long as it runs fast" is an answer: keep it unless someone shows fast without it, and nobody has. So B is out on your own terms, which the brief also concluded.

**5, run-time coercion in the interpreter.** The spec says the checker decides at compile time where a coercion goes; the compiled path does that already. The interpreter has no checker, so it can only find out at run time, at dispatch: when no overload matches, try the declared coercions. Same program, same answer in the normal case, the choice made later; that is the divergence. Not the class loader (that is the compiled path's). JIT: not relevant here, the interpreter is our oracle, not the target, and its speed is irrelevant by your rule. On the compiled path a coercion is a static call to a small function, inlined by the JIT, costing the boxing every operation pays today until unboxing lands. Can it run first: yes, that is A's first rung, 150 to 200 lines in six interpreter files, no library line changed, the gate green throughout because today's tower needs no coercion.

- **A touches only the library and the interpreter.** Its two rungs are the interpreter coercion mechanism and the 14 rewritten headers. C's checker half (the forest test in `checkP`, `comprises T` on seven traits, the return-type rule) is independent of that and can be added at any later time.
- **Going A then C costs one library rung in reverse.** Re-nesting means restoring the 14 `extends` links from the record (the keep note's sketch lists them), about the same size as A's library rung, and deciding what `Number`'s catch-alls become. Under remedy (i) no test or program text was changed, so there is nothing to undo there; the flat sketch is fully documented.
- **The coercion rung is not wasted either way.** The spec has coercion regardless of the tower's shape, the compiler prelude uses it, and the interpreter lacking it is a gap under every route. Under a re-nested tower the width coercions simply stop firing.
- **What is lost on a reversal:** A's library rung, about half of A's cost (1.6 M by batch 3's rate), plus the recorded spec deviation and its tests, plus any output changes accepted in between. The other order, C then A, throws away C's derived rule and checker work instead, which is the larger and less certain piece.
- **C can stay alive cheaply without being the route.** Its checker half exists as a measured shadow; the missing piece, the return-type rule, can be probed on a branch with the nested tower whenever you want it tested, without touching `main`.

The one genuine one-way element is the switch-over itself: once the compiler checks the one library in A's shape, code written for the compiled path afterwards assumes it. A return to C then also re-checks that code. A probe of C's rule before the switch-over would tell you whether that door is worth keeping open.

content.text:
Not stupid; the record answers it, and the answer is "he didn't, and the tool didn't exist".

- **The nested tower is 2008 library code, not Steele's design.** It begins with `ZZ32 extends { StandardTotalOrder[\ZZ32\], ZZ64 }` on 2008-05-06 (Jan-Willem Maessen's commit) and is complete by 2008-07-21. Steele's own hand on the numbers is the opposite move: he flattened the compiler prelude's tower in July 2011.
- **In 2008 the library was written for the interpreter, and the interpreter has no coercion.** Coercion in Fortress is a static mechanism: the checker inserts it where no declaration fits. The interpreter runs no checker, then or now, so subtyping was the only way to make `1 - beta1` or `SQRT 5` work at all. Nesting was the available tool, not a choice against coercion.
- **It matched the spec's picture.** The spec states ℤ inside ℚ inside ℝ as subtyping and reserves coercion for the machine widths (`ZZ64 coerce(z: ZZ32)` is its example). The library went further than the spec and nested the machine widths too. Fortress's coercion is also deliberately weak, tried last and never chained, so it is a poorer widening tool than Java's; that made subtyping the more attractive spelling.
- **Run-time dispatch made it cheap.** With multiple dispatch on values, one body on `Number` serves every number; the library's own comment on its reductions says it: "Hack to permit any Number to work non-parametrically".
- **The constraints that break it came later.** The exclusion rule entered the checker in 2010, the specialisation shortcut in 2011. When the compiled world hit the conflict, the team wrote its library flat with coercion, the well-trodden path from Java. The interpreter's library was never revised, because the compiler never got far enough to check it.

So the flat path is well trodden in other languages; in Fortress it existed only in the prelude, and the nested tower is the earlier, interpreter-only answer that the team's compiler work overtook without going back to fix.
